activities.caption: keeps the balance or tips the see-saw?
activities.name: eqBalanceSort

config.prompt: File each move under what it does to the balanced see-saw:

items.label: add 3 to the left side only
divide both sides by x — the unknown

config.why: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other — and never divide by the unknown, which silently discards solutions.

config.prompt: Pair each tidying skill with the move that performs it:

pairs.right: evaluate the general rule for a chosen value

config.why: Factorising matters because factors reveal structure: the factored form shows instantly that x² − 9 is zero when x = 3 or x = −3.

activities.anchor: a minus sign in front of brackets affects only the first term
activities.caption: find the sign slip
activities.name: eqMinusSpot

config.prompt: One of these expansions is wrong — click it:
lines: In 3 − (x + 2), the minus multiplies everything inside the brackets.
config.why: Distribute the −1 like any other coefficient, then collect like terms — sign slips at exactly this spot are among the most common errors in school algebra.

config.prompt: Rebuild the solution of 2(x + 5) = 3x − 4 — what comes first:
items: Check by substituting back: both sides give 38
config.why: Undo in reverse order, then check by substituting back — the ten-second habit that catches most algebra slips ever made.

config.root: x² = x. A student divides both sides by x and reports x = 1. What went wrong?

choices.label: Nothing — the answer is correct
choices.feedback: It is correct but incomplete: dividing by x silently discarded the second solution, x = 0.

choices.label: Dividing by the unknown keeps only some solutions — factorise instead
choices.feedback: x(x − 1) = 0 keeps both answers: x = 0 and x = 1.

choices.label: The error was squaring something
choices.feedback: No squaring happened here — the discarded root came from dividing by the unknown.

lost.text: One root survives; the other was divided away without a trace.

factor.text: Factorise — x(x − 1) = 0 — and both answers survive.

no.text: The culprit is the division by x, not any squaring.

config.why: Never divide by the unknown: factorise instead, so no solution is silently discarded.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the formula that solves every quadratic
activities.name: eqQuadCloze

config.text: The quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(%%0%%)) / %%1%%a solves ax² + bx + c = 0 for any coefficients, and the discriminant — the part under the root — tells you how many real answers exist: two, %%2%%, or none.
config.hint: What sits under the square root, what divides it, and the middle possibility for the root count.

activities.anchor: But multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the famous flip
activities.name: eqFlipPredict

config.q: From −2x > 10, dividing both sides by −2 gives…
choices: x = −5 — the comparison becomes an equation
config.why: Multiplying by −1 turns 'greater' into 'less': 3 > 2 is true, yet −3 < −2. Forgetting the flip is the single most common inequality error in existence.

activities.caption: two routes, one destination — drag the divider
activities.name: eqSimulCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to solve 2x + y = 11 and x − y = 1 — drag the divider:

before.label: elimination
before.text: add the two equations so the y terms cancel — 3x = 12, so x = 4, then y = 3

after.label: substitution
after.text: the second equation says y = x − 1; insert that into the first and solve

config.why: Two routes, one destination — and either answer can be checked in both original equations (8 + 3 = 11; 4 − 3 = 1).

config.prompt: One of these graph readings is backwards — click it:
lines: A distance–time graph's gradient is speed.
Where two cost graphs intersect is where the more expensive option always wins.
config.correction: Where two graphs intersect is where two options become equal — the break-even point.
config.why: The crossing is where one courier's flat fee beats the other's per-km rate — which option wins depends on which side of it you are.

config.prompt: The geometric sequence 2, 6, 18, 54 multiplies by 3 each step. Roughly what is its 7th term?
config.why: 2 × 3⁶ = 1,458 — the shape of compound interest and population growth, exploding upward whenever r > 1.
config.context: the general term is aₙ = a₁ × rⁿ⁻¹
